title: Ex 3.4 #8 · Odd digits in one unbroken run
prompt: Use each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 exactly once to form a 7-digit number in which the odd digits 1, 3, 5, 7 appear together in one unbroken run. For example, 2753146 qualifies, but 1234567 does not. How many such numbers are there?
answer_format: A whole number, or an expression for it like 26^4, 10!/7! or binom(10, 3). P(n, k) and C(n, k) work too.

mistakes.hint: You arranged the odd digits and the even digits, but the run itself can sit in different places: treat it as one big symbol arranged along with 2, 4 and 6.
The even digits outside the run can also come in different orders.
That counts every arrangement of the seven digits, including ones where the odd digits are split up.

hints: Glue the four odd digits into a single block. Then you are arranging that block together with 2, 4 and 6.
Count the orders of the four items (the block, 2, 4, 6), then the orders of the odd digits inside the block.
solution: Treat the run of odd digits as one block. Arranging the block with the three even digits means arranging 4 items: $4! = 24$ ways.
Inside the block, the digits 1, 3, 5, 7 can be in any order: $4! = 24$ ways.
By the multiplication principle there are $4! \cdot 4! = 576$ such numbers.

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses factorials and the multiplication principle (Section 3.4).
